personality_voice.book_baseline: In the books, Ron is defined by a cluster of observable traits: loyal and instinctively protective of Harry and Hermione; quick to laugh (he 'roared with laughter' at Harry blowing up Aunt Marge, finds Trelawney's class absurd); direct, sometimes blunt to the point of cruelty (mocking Hermione about the Grim, dismissing Divination with sarcasm); stubborn and emotionally reactive (prolonged silence toward Hermione over Crookshanks, sustained fury at Scabbers's apparent death); brave when it counts but openly cowardly about spiders; and capable of genuine warmth expressed awkwardly (patting Hermione 'very awkwardly on the top of the head,' offering to make tea for Hagrid because 'it's what my mum does'). His speech patterns are colloquial, often impulsive, peppered with exclamations ('RON -- WEASLEY!', 'BLOOD!', 'LOOK!'), rhetorical deflation ('You're both mental'), and self-aware humor ('She's gone mental, Hermione has. I mean, not that she wasn't always mental'). He exhibits a canonical insecurity about his family's poverty and his position in Harry's shadow, but the books express this through reactive resentment rather than explicit complaint. His voice is recognizably lower-middle-register: unpretentious, emotionally unguarded, funny without intending to be.
personality_voice.film_portrayal: The film preserves the core comedic, loyal, and impulsively reactive Ron. His dialogue retains the broad register: 'I'm warning you, Hermione! Keep that bloody beast of yours away from Scabbers or I'll turn it into a tea cozy,' 'A cat! Is that what they told you? Looks more like a pig with hair,' 'Let me get this straight. Sirius Black escaped from Azkaban to come after you?' and his running commentary on the Dementor encounter ('Well, you sort of went... rigid. We thought maybe you were having a fit or something'). His fear of spiders is dramatised faithfully in the Boggart lesson. His protective instinct appears in 'If you want to kill Harry, you'll have to kill us too!' (transferred in form from the book to Hermione, but Ron's version remains in the film — though notably Hermione delivers it first). His sardonic humor survives: 'She's gone mental, Hermione has. I mean, not that she wasn't always mental, but now it's out in the open for everyone to see.' His awkward physical comedy is present throughout.
personality_voice.difference: Several secondary traits are reduced or absent. The book's Ron has a notable competitive streak about family pride and social anxiety — his extended fury over Hermione's perceived betrayals (Firebolt, Scabbers) is present but compressed, losing the sustained texture of weeks of cold treatment. The film strips out the sustained Crookshanks-Scabbers conflict that occupies multiple chapters and defines Ron's stubborn streak at length. His comment to Snape's class ('He's got a point, you know') when Snape calls Hermione a know-it-all is a film-specific moment that slightly softens his canonical defense of her in the same scene (in the book he loudly defends Hermione, earning detention). The film Ron is somewhat more generically reactive and comedic, with less of the sustained emotional stubbornness that defines book-Ron across whole stretches of the year. The 'make tea for Hagrid' moment — a quietly defining detail of his emotional intelligence — is absent. His speech still retains recognisable patterns but is less densely characterised.
personality_voice.penalty_logic: The core personality is preserved and the dominant traits — loyalty, humor, fear of spiders, bluntness, protectiveness, and emotional reactivity — are all directly evidenced in the film corpus. The loss is in secondary-layer consistency: sustained stubbornness, the specific blend of jealousy and warmth, the awkward tenderness. No major trait is inverted or newly invented. A score in the 18–22 range is appropriate: main personality preserved, but some simplification and loss of secondary texture.

narrative_role_agency.book_baseline: In the books, Ron performs several distinct structural functions in PoA. He is Harry's primary emotional sounding board and social anchor. He is the one who pushes Harry toward agency when Hermione is cautious (urging Harry to ask McGonagall for Hogsmeade permission, being the one to suggest visiting Hagrid, enabling Harry's Hogsmeade trips). He is the plot's key physical link to Pettigrew: Scabbers is his rat, the discovery of Pettigrew's identity is inseparable from Ron's ownership of and relationship with Scabbers. In the Shrieking Shack, Ron's moral agency is central: despite a broken leg, he physically positions himself between Black and Harry, saying 'If you want to kill Harry, you'll have to kill us too!' — a willful act of protection. He also, alongside Hermione, disarms Snape (both fire Expelliarmus simultaneously). He is repeatedly the one who observes threats (wiping the window on the train, noticing Scabbers's distress). He drives the Buckbeak defense research in the latter half of the book.
narrative_role_agency.film_portrayal: The film preserves Ron as Harry's sidekick and emotional companion. His link to Scabbers and Pettigrew remains structurally intact — Ron is still the rat's owner and the Pettigrew revelation goes through him. He still says a version of the 'have to kill us too' line. He is present at all key scenes. His observation role on the train is preserved ('There's something moving out there'). However, his agency is systematically reduced. In the film, Hermione delivers 'If you want to kill Harry, you'll have to kill us too!' first and most forcefully, with Ron's version muted. In the Shrieking Shack scene, Ron's role is largely reactive and passive — he mostly observes. His active push for Harry's Hogsmeade trips is absent from the film (the Hogsmeade logistics are simplified). His sustained effort on the Buckbeak defense research — which in the books represents a major independent contribution — is entirely absent from the film. The Expelliarmus-alongside-Hermione moment against Snape is absent from the film (Harry alone disarms Snape in the film version).
narrative_role_agency.difference: Several meaningful acts of agency are removed or transferred: (1) Ron's sustained Buckbeak defense research is cut entirely — Hermione retains it. (2) Ron's Expelliarmus co-discharge against Snape is cut; Harry alone does it. (3) Ron's active role in pushing Harry toward Hogsmeade visits is compressed or removed. (4) Hermione now leads the 'have to kill us too' declaration. Ron's injury and sacrifice at the Whomping Willow — releasing Harry's hands deliberately — is preserved and is effective. His role as Pettigrew's vessel remains. But the transfer of his research agency to Hermione and the removal of his Expelliarmus co-action represent meaningful losses per the Transfer Rule.
narrative_role_agency.penalty_logic: Ron's role as Pettigrew's keeper and his protective sacrifice at the Willow are intact. But multiple acts of initiative are transferred (research) or cut (Expelliarmus with Hermione, Hogsmeade encouragement). The cap at 75 for transferred agency applies here alongside the reduction in the score. The role is 'reduced but recognizable' per the 14–17 band.

motivations_internal_conflict.book_baseline: Ron's motivations in PoA are layered and consistent. He is motivated by loyalty to Harry above all, which produces genuine conflict when Harry's safety pulls against other considerations. His protectiveness of Scabbers stems from genuine affection for an old pet and from the insecurity of owning secondhand things ('like nearly everything Ron owned, Scabbers the rat was secondhand'). His sustained anger at Hermione over Crookshanks is motivated by a real sense of injustice combined with difficulty articulating grief. His desire to see Buckbeak saved is genuine and stems from loyalty to Hagrid, not obligation. His most complex motivational moment is when he debates whether to tell Harry about Black's pursuit: he clearly wants to protect Harry but also fears being unable to do so. His internal conflict when confronted with Pettigrew is visible: he is disgusted ('I let you sleep in my bed!'), but also briefly at sea — he clings to Scabbers even after the evidence accumulates, because the alternative is too destabilising.
motivations_internal_conflict.film_portrayal: The film captures Ron's loyalty to Harry and his instinct for protection fairly well. His protectiveness of Scabbers is conveyed through the Crookshanks conflict. His disgust at Pettigrew in the Shrieking Shack ('You're mad,' drawing back in revulsion) is shown. His motivation to protect Harry at the Whomping Willow — sacrificing himself — is present and affecting. However, several motivational layers are absent. The poverty-and-secondhand-things dimension of his attachment to Scabbers is entirely absent from the film, removing the subtext that makes the Crookshanks conflict richer. His internal conflict over Buckbeak's defense — the guilt at having forgotten it, the sustained effort to make it right — is absent. His ambivalence when confronted with proof about Pettigrew is present but brief, lacking the extended wrestling shown in the books.
motivations_internal_conflict.difference: The film preserves the correct motivational direction (loyalty, protectiveness, friendship) but strips the socioeconomic subtext and the guilt/redemption arc around Buckbeak. The core motivations are recognizable but simplified.
motivations_internal_conflict.penalty_logic: Motivations are simplified but still correct in direction. This fits the 11–13 band: 'Motivations are simplified but still correct.' No motivations are inverted or replaced with wrong ones.

character_arc.book_baseline: Ron's arc in PoA is modest but real. He begins the book somewhat immature (shouting on the telephone, fighting over Crookshanks and Scabbers at length, being petty toward Percy), and over the course of the year he grows through several tests. The Buckbeak research represents Ron independently taking on adult responsibility. His sustained anger at Hermione ends in genuine reconciliation, initiated not by Ron fully capitulating but by shared grief over Hagrid's loss. His most important arc moment is in the Shrieking Shack: despite a broken leg, he offers himself as protection for Harry, and his response to Pettigrew ('I let you sleep in my bed!') represents a specific moral clarity about betrayal. By year's end he extends genuine friendship offers to Harry for the summer (Quidditch World Cup), showing deepened investment in maintaining their bond through adversity.
character_arc.film_portrayal: The film compresses Ron's arc substantially. The early immaturity is present (Crookshanks/Scabbers conflict, reactive arguments). The Buckbeak research arc is eliminated entirely, removing Ron's most sustained act of independent growth. The reconciliation with Hermione is dramatically compressed: it happens via a Hagrid-forced handshake/hug scene, which is well-executed but replaces the organic, earned reconciliation of the book. The Shrieking Shack sacrifice is preserved and effective. The year-end warmth with Harry is present ('I'll call you about the World Cup' is not shown in the film corpus, though Sirius's letter and the owl gift arrive). Ron ends the film in largely the same place he started, emotionally — loyal, funny, somewhat reactive — without a clear sense of growth having been depicted.
character_arc.difference: The arc's most developed step (Buckbeak research as moral reparation) is entirely absent. The reconciliation with Hermione is intact in outcome but simplified in process. The arc's final note is present in the Shrieking Shack but the connective tissue of growth is thinned. The arc is 'incomplete, rushed, or missing important steps' — fitting the 8–10 band, but the Shack sacrifice and emotional endpoint preserve enough that 11 is defensible.
character_arc.penalty_logic: The arc exists and its most important moment (sacrifice at the Shack) is preserved, but the developmental steps through the year are significantly shortened. This fits the lower end of the 11–13 band ('compressed but still faithful') or the upper end of 8–10 ('incomplete, missing important steps'). The Buckbeak-research omission is the most significant loss.

key_relationships.book_baseline: Ron's key relationships in PoA are: (1) Harry — primary companion, equal partner in courage, emotionally frank; Ron pushes Harry, argues with him, and sacrifices for him. (2) Hermione — a friendship defined by mutual irritation, mutual respect, and genuine warmth barely expressed; the Crookshanks/Scabbers conflict is the year's central relational stress for this pair, resolved through shared grief and awkward tenderness. (3) Scabbers — not a relationship in the narrative sense, but Ron's attachment to this rat reveals his loyalty, his grief, his insecurity (secondhand, useless, but mine). (4) Hagrid — genuine, warm, expressed through actions (visiting, defending Buckbeak). The Ron-Hermione dynamic is especially important: the books invest chapters in sustained cold silence, petty arguments, and eventual collapse into reconciliation, showing that both characters are too similar in stubbornness to simply forgive and forget.
key_relationships.film_portrayal: The Harry-Ron dynamic is generally preserved: they are co-conspirators, Ron supports Harry and argues with him. The Hermione-Ron conflict over Crookshanks/Scabbers exists in the film and produces real friction, but the sustained cold-shoulder treatment spanning weeks is compressed into a few scenes. The Hagrid relationship is present. The Ron-Scabbers attachment lacks the 'secondhand things' texture. The film's reconciliation scene — Hagrid forcing a hug — is a different emotional mechanism than the book's organic resolution through shared crisis and Hermione's genuine apology over Scabbers. The forced-hug approach makes the reconciliation externally imposed rather than internally motivated, slightly changing the dynamic of both characters.
key_relationships.difference: The Harry-Ron dynamic is largely preserved. The Hermione-Ron dynamic is present but compressed and the reconciliation mechanism is changed: it is now externally mediated by Hagrid rather than arising organically. The loss of the 'secondhand things' texture affects the Ron-Scabbers dynamic. These are not inversions but meaningful compressions.
key_relationships.penalty_logic: Relationships are 'mostly faithful, with some compression or simplification' — fits the 7–8 band. The Hermione-Ron reconciliation mechanism change is a meaningful difference but not a fundamental inversion of the emotional dynamic.

complexity_nuance_lost_material.book_baseline: The books give Ron significant complexity in PoA that goes beyond his surface role. (1) The socioeconomic subtext: his secondhand things, his embarrassment about his family's poverty, his reliance on inherited pets — these give his reactions texture that makes him more than 'the funny sidekick.' (2) His jealousy and insecurity are real and not always flattering: he can be petty (his sustained cold treatment of Hermione is excessive even by his own standards), and he is aware of it. (3) His instinct for emotional care is shown in small, understated moments: offering to make tea, knowing that 'it's what my mum does when someone's upset.' (4) His interaction with Sir Cadogan — 'Yeah, we'll call you... if we ever need someone mental' — shows dry humor alongside genuine impatience. (5) His complexity in the Scabbers saga: he is both the one most attached to Scabbers and the one who most loudly dismisses him as boring and useless, a contradiction that reveals emotional self-protection. (6) His moral clarity when confronted with Pettigrew ('I let you sleep in my bed!') is sharp and specific. (7) His extended research on Buckbeak shows initiative that is never visible in his typical characterization. (8) The sustained weeks-long cold war with Hermione shows a stubborn streak that is neither wholly sympathetic nor unsympathetic.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.film_portrayal: The film preserves Ron's humor, loyalty, fear of spiders, impulsiveness, and the Pettigrew-disgust moment. However, it loses: the socioeconomic subtext entirely; the 'make tea' emotional intelligence moment; the weeks-long cold war texture with Hermione; the Buckbeak research; the sustained contradiction of dismissing Scabbers while grieving him; and the nuanced awkwardness of the Hermione reconciliation. The 'He's got a point, you know' moment in the Snape class replaces the book's more complex defense of Hermione, and while amusing, it slightly flattens Ron's protectiveness into a comedy beat.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.difference: The film Ron is recognizable but flatter — primarily comic, loyal, and reactive, without the socioeconomic texture, the self-aware stubbornness, the understated emotional intelligence, or the independent initiative. The complexity that comes from his contradictions (dismissing Scabbers while loving him, being petty while being brave, being funny while being emotionally astute) is significantly reduced.
complexity_nuance_lost_material.penalty_logic: This is a noticeable simplification: important nuances, subtext, and the contradiction-driven texture of book-Ron are missing. This fits the 8–10 band ('noticeable simplification; important nuances, relationships, agency, or contradictions are missing'). The character is not reduced to a single trait — he retains humor, loyalty, and some emotional complexity — but the richer book material is largely gone.

Ron's co-Expelliarmus with Hermione against Snape (cut; Harry alone disarms Snape in the film)
Ron's socioeconomic subtext — the 'secondhand things' texture tied to Scabbers, his wand, his possessions
Ron offering to make tea for Hagrid and explaining 'It's what my mum does when someone's upset'
The weeks-long sustained cold war with Hermione over Crookshanks/Scabbers (compressed to a few scenes)
Ron's organic reconciliation with Hermione — initiated by Hermione's apology and shared grief; replaced in the film by Hagrid-imposed hug
Ron's contradictory Scabbers attachment (simultaneously dismissing and grieving him across chapters)
Ron's initiative in pushing Harry to ask McGonagall for Hogsmeade permission and enabling his secret Hogsmeade visits
The specific 'I let you sleep in my bed!' line of moral clarity — present in the film only in a compressed form
Ron being made a celebrity after Black's dormitory break-in and relishing the attention

score_caps_applied: Cap 3 (score above 75 if one or more core book functions, decisions, or acts of agency transferred to another character): Applied — Ron's Buckbeak research and Expelliarmus co-action transferred to Hermione/Harry respectively. Total held below 75.
Cap 1 (score above 85 if films remove a major part of complexity, agency, or narrative function): Applied — but total already below 85 due to other penalties.
key_observations: The film's Ron Weasley is a faithful surface reproduction: the humor, the loyalty, the spider fear, the protectiveness, and the emotional impulsiveness are all preserved and recognizable. However, the adaptation systematically strips the secondary layer that makes book-Ron complex: his socioeconomic subtext, his sustained stubbornness, his understated emotional intelligence, his independent research initiative, and the textured contradiction of loving what he dismisses. Two meaningful acts of agency are lost or transferred — the Buckbeak research goes entirely to Hermione, and the joint Expelliarmus against Snape becomes Harry's alone. The Ron-Hermione reconciliation is changed from an organic emotional event to a Hagrid-mediated physical gesture. The result is a Ron who is funny, warm, and brave on screen but significantly flatter than on the page — a character whose core identity survives but whose richness, contradictions, and moral interiority are substantially reduced.
